subject: Business Models
title: The Free Trial Hook
description: Learn The Free Trial Hook in one minute.

hook.text: Start your free 30-day trial—credit card required. 80% of people who sign up forget to cancel.

buildup.text: Free trials lower the barrier to entry. Once usage becomes habitual, cancellation feels like a loss.

discovery.text: The 'endowment effect' kicks in: people value what they already have more than what they might gain.

twist.text: The FTC now requires companies to make canceling as easy as signing up. Many still bury the option.

climax.text: Free trials convert 25-60% of users to paid, depending on the product's habit-forming design.

punchline.text: Try free, forget to cancel, pay forever. The trial is the trap.

quiz.question: What psychological effect makes free trials effective?

details.summary: Free trials offer full product access for a limited period, typically 7 to 30 days, before automatically converting to a paid subscription. The strategy relies on users experiencing enough value during the trial to justify the recurring charge, or simply forgetting to cancel before billing begins.
details.whyItMatters: Free trials are the primary acquisition tool for subscription businesses. Conversion rates from trial to paid range from 2% to 60% depending on product category and trial design..
takeaways: Limited time access converts users into paying subscribers after the trial
Trial-to-paid conversion is the critical metric for trial-based acquisition
Requiring payment upfront increases conversion but decreases trial starts

faq.question: What design decisions most impact free trial conversion rates?
faq.answer: Requiring a credit card upfront increases conversion to 50-60% from trial because inertia works in the company's favor. No-card trials convert at 2-10% but attract more trial starts. Trial length matters: too short prevents value discovery, too long reduces urgency to buy.

faq.question: Is it ethical to auto-charge after free trials expire?
faq.answer: Auto-charging after clear disclosure and consent is standard practice. However, intentionally obscuring the transition date, making cancellation difficult, or targeting vulnerable populations raises ethical concerns. Transparency about charges and easy cancellation options maintain trust.
